claim: 2% dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced acute experimental colitis results in no significant alterations in the levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), and bilirubin on day 6 of DSS treatment in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Analysis of biochemical parameters on day 6 of DSS treatment showed no significant alterations in the levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), and bilirubin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurements presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a showing no significant changes in liver damage markers.

claim: Histological studies of liver tissues from DSS-treated C57BL/6 mice showed neither morphological differences nor any hepatocellular fibrosis.
source: Furthermore, histological studies of these treated liver tissues from C57BL/6 mice showed neither morphological differences nor any hepatocellular fibrosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological examination data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Liver functionalities are maintained and no major damage in the liver tissue occurs in the colitogenic mice model.
source: Thus, in general, the liver functionalities are maintained and no major damage in the liver tissue occurs in the colitogenic mice model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical and histological data showing no significant liver damage.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of transcriptome data segregated DSS-treated and control samples on PC1 with a variance of 53%.
source: Unsupervised clustering of the transcriptome data by principal component analysis (PCA) segregated the treated and control samples on PC1 with a variance of 53% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: LPS-mediated signaling in the liver was identified as among the key differentially expressed systems in DSS-treated mice.
source: LPS-mediated signaling in the liver was identified as among the key differentially expressed systems (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Microbial components, including LPS from the gut, can reach the liver through portal blood, activating the hepatic immune response during colitis-mediated barrier impairment.
source: It is proposed that microbial components, including LPS from the gut, can reach the liver through portal blood, activating the hepatic immune response during colitis-mediated barrier impairment.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on established knowledge of gut-liver communication.

claim: Rela and Stat3 are two important transcription factors activated by the microbial LPS.
source: Interestingly, Rela and Stat3 are two important transcription factors activated by the microbial LPS and these two pathways frequently converge to elicit protective responses (Balic et al., 2020; Sakai et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2016; Ahyi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcript abundance of Rela, Stat3, and other downstream genes was higher in the DSS-treated group compared to the control.
source: Further analysis of the transcript abundance of Rela, Stat3, and other downstream genes reflected higher transcript abundance in the DSS-treated group as compared to the control (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Immunostaining studies showed an enhanced signal intensity of p-Rela (Ser536), p-Stat3 (Ser727), and p-Stat3 (Tyr705) in DSS-treated liver sections compared to untreated samples.
source: Immunostaining studies showed an enhanced signal intensity of p-Rela (Ser536), p-Stat3 (Ser727), and p-Stat3 (Tyr705) in the treated liver sections, as compared to untreated samples (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RelA phosphorylation at Ser536 peaks at day 2 (about eightfold increase) following DSS treatment, with a two to threefold increase sustained till day 6.
source: The RelA phosphorylation at Ser536 peaks at day 2 (about eightfold increase) following which a two to threefold increase was sustained till day 6 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Stat3 phosphorylation at Ser727 increases gradually from day 2 (eightfold) to day 6 (17-fold) following DSS treatment.
source: The Stat3 phosphorylation at Ser727 increases gradually from day 2 (eightfold) to day 6 (17-fold).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Stat3 tyrosine phosphorylation is transient and can be detected at day 4 (ninefold) post-DSS treatment.
source: Tyrosine phosphorylation, on the other hand, is transient and can be detected at day 4 (ninefold) post-treatment (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: A marked reduction in pStat3 (Ser727) levels occurs post-antibiotic treatment in colitogenic wild-type mice.
source: A marked reduction in pStat3 (Ser727) levels post-antibiotic treatment in the colitogenic wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e) could be noted, suggesting that optimal endotoxin flux may be a major driver of hepatic Rela/Stat3 signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Optimal endotoxin flux may be a major driver of hepatic Rela/Stat3 signaling.
source: A marked reduction in pStat3 (Ser727) levels post-antibiotic treatment in the colitogenic wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e) could be noted, suggesting that optimal endotoxin flux may be a major driver of hepatic Rela/Stat3 signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that antibiotic treatment reduces pStat3 levels.

claim: RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice were almost resistant to induction of colitis, with only a minor increase in the disease activity index (DAI) on day 6 post-onset of DSS treatment.
source: Surprisingly, RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice were almost resistant to induction of colitis, and only a minor increase in the DAI could be seen on day 6 post-onset of DSS treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DAI measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DSS treatment for 6 days showed substantial shortening of the colon length in wild-type, RelaΔhep, and Stat3Δhep mice, but not in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Concurrently, DSS treatment for 6 days showed substantial shortening of the colon length in wild-type, RelaΔhep, and Stat3Δhep mice, but not in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by colon length measurements shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Wild-type animals showed a 12-fold increase in FITC-dextran in the serum, while RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed a substantially lower, fivefold increase.
source: A 12-fold increase in FITC-dextran in the serum of the wild-type animals was seen, while the RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed a substantially lower, fivefold increase (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FITC-dextran permeability assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DSS treatment led to extensive disruption of the intestinal crypts and depletion of the mucin layer in wild-type mice, accompanied by submucosal leukocyte infiltration.
source: DSS treatment led to extensive disruption of the intestinal crypts and depletion of the mucin layer in wild-type mice, accompanied by submucosal leukocyte infiltration.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed substantially attenuated epithelial changes along with minimal erosion of mucin layers following DSS treatment.
source: In contrast, RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed substantially attenuated epithelial changes along with minimal erosion of mucin layers (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DSS treatment of wild-type mice triggered a two-and-a-half-fold and twofold reduction in the colonic abundance of enterocyte markers, tight junction 1 (Tjp1), and occludin (Ocln), respectively.
source: RT-qPCR analysis revealed that DSS treatment of wild-type mice triggered a two-and-a-half-fold and twofold reduction in the colonic abundance of enterocyte markers, tight junction 1 (Tjp1), and occludin (Ocln), respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DSS treatment of wild-type mice resulted in a fourfold and twofold decrease in the colonic abundance of goblet cell markers, mucins-2, and trefoil factor 3 (Tff3), respectively.
source: Similarly, we noticed a fourfold and twofold decrease in the colonic abundance of goblet cell markers, mucins-2, and trefoil factor 3 (Tff3), respectively, in wild-type mice upon DSS treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Except for a moderate decrease in the Tjp1 mRNA level, none of the enterocyte or goblet cell markers were downregulated upon DSS treatment in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Except for a moderate decrease in the Tjp1 mRNA level, none of these mRNAs were downregulated upon DSS treatment in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The absence of Rela and Stat3 in hepatocytes protects mice from DSS-induced colitis.
source: Taken together these studies reveal intriguing observations wherein the absence of Rela and Stat3 in hepatocytes protects mice from DSS-induced colitis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations including DAI, colon length, histology, and gene expression data.

claim: On day 4 and day 6 post DSS-treatment, ALT, AST, GGT, and bilirubin levels were within the physiological range in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice, indicating no apparent damage to the liver.
source: On day 4 and day 6 post DSS-treatment, ALT, AST, GGT, and bilirubin levels were within the physiological range, indicating no apparent damage to the liver (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Histological studies suggested no morphological differences in the DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Similarly, the histological studies also suggested no morphological differences in the DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Liver functions are maintained in the colitogenic RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice, similar to that observed in the wild-type animals.
source: In conclusion, the above data indicates that the liver functions are maintained in the colitogenic RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice, similar to that observed in the wild-type animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on biochemical and histological data.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of transcriptomic data using PCA segregates wild-type and RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice samples subjected to DSS treatment.
source: Unsupervised clustering of transcriptomic data using the PCA tool segregates wild-type and RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice samples subjected to DSS treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Untreated mice from the wild-type and RelaΔhepStat3Δhep cluster together in the PCA plot.
source: Notably, untreated mice from the wild-type and RelaΔhepStat3Δhep cluster together in the PCA plot.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Comparative pathway enrichment analysis showed differences in the acute phase responses, bile acid metabolic processes, response to ER stress, and one-carbon metabolism between wild-type and RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice upon DSS treatment.
source: Comparative pathway enrichment analysis using GO terms for differentially expressed genes in the liver upon DSS treatment between wild-type and RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed differences in the acute phase responses, bile acid metabolic processes, response to ER stress, and one-carbon metabolism (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BA dysmetabolism has been reported in IBD patients by several studies and is also recapitulated in the mice models.
source: BA dysmetabolism has been reported in IBD patients by several studies and is also recapitulated in the mice models (Zhou and Hylemon, 2014; Bromke and Krzystek-Korpacka, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The levels of secondary BAs are lower, and primary BAs are elevated in IBD because of impairment of microbiota-mediated deconjugation and transformation activities.
source: The consensus thesis is that the levels of secondary BAs are lower, and primary BAs are elevated because of impairment of microbiota-mediated deconjugation and transformation activities.
evidence: This is a statement of consensus from the literature.

claim: Analysis from colonic biopsies of IBD subjects showed elevated levels of primary BAs.
source: Concordantly, our analysis from colonic biopsies of IBD subjects also showed elevated levels of primary BAs (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS data from human IBD biopsies shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Transcriptomics data showed downregulation of Cyp7b1 in the RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice and the other biosynthesis enzymes also follow a similar trend.
source: Transcriptomics data strikingly showed downregulation of Cyp7b1 in the RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice and the other biosynthesis enzymes also follow a similar trend (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–e.

claim: In comparison to DSS-treated wild-type mice, DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice expressed a reduced level of mRNAs encoding primary bile acid synthesis pathway enzymes Cyp7a1, Cyp8b1, Cyp27a1, and Cyp7b1 in the liver.
source: Our RT-qPCR analyses substantiated that in comparison to DSS-treated wild-type mice, DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice expressed a reduced level of mRNAs encoding primary bile acid synthesis pathway enzymes Cyp7a1, Cyp8b1, Cyp27a1, and Cyp7b1 in the liver (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hepatic Rela and Stat3 instruct a gene program in the liver of colitogenic mice that supports the expression of mRNAs encoding primary BA metabolism enzymes.
source: Thus, our data propose a new hypothesis that hepatic Rela and Stat3 instruct a gene program in the liver of colitogenic mice that supports the expression of mRNAs encoding primary BA metabolism enzymes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed downregulation of bile acid synthesis enzymes in knockout mice.

claim: The abundance of cholic acid in the liver was approximately sevenfold less in DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice compared to their wild-type counterparts.
source: Our analyses revealed the abundance of cholic acid in the liver, which was approximately sevenfold less in DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted LC-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A close to 10-fold decrease in the hepatic level of CDCA was observed in DSS-treated knockout mice.
source: Likewise, we captured a close to 10-fold decrease in the hepatic level of CDCA in DSS-treated knockout mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted LC-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Substantially reduced levels of ursodeoxycholic acid and α-muricholic acid were observed in DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: A substantially reduced levels of ursodeoxycholic acid and α-muricholic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted LC-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A significantly reduced accumulation of both CA and CDCA was found in the colon of DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Consistent with the levels observed in the liver, we found a significantly reduced accumulation of both CA and CDCA in the colon of DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted LC-MS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference between wild-type and knockout mice was substantially more marked for CDCA in the colon.
source: The difference between wild-type and knockout mice was substantially more marked for CDCA (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted LC-MS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CDCA has been reported to engage the NLRP3 inflammasome, causing liver inflammation during cholestasis.
source: CDCA has been reported to engage the NLRP3 inflammasome, causing liver inflammation during cholestasis (Gong et al., 2016.)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ex vivo experiments have shown that CDCA induces pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion by intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Furthermore, ex vivo experiments have shown that CDCA induces pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion by intestinal epithelial cells (Horikawa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Compared to DSS-treated wild-type mice, DSS-treated knockout mice presented with substantially reduced levels of mRNAs encoding key pro-inflammatory cytokines, namely Il1b, Tnfa, and Il6.
source: Indeed, compared to DSS-treated wild-type mice, DSS-treated knockout mice presented with substantially reduced levels of mRNAs encoding key pro-inflammatory cytokines, namely Il1b, Tnfa, and Il6 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice displayed a diminished frequency of inflammatory effector immune cells in the colitogenic gut.
source: Consistent with the less inflamed intestinal milieu, RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice also displayed a diminished frequency of inflammatory effector immune cells in the colitogenic gut (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Confocal microscopy-based analyses depicted a close to fivefold reduction in the recruitment of Ly6G+ cells, including neutrophils and monocytes, F4/80+ macrophages, and CD11c+ including macrophages and the dendritic cells in DSS-treated knockout mice, compared to their wild-type counterparts.
source: Confocal microscopy-based analyses of stained colon sections depicted a close to fivefold reduction in the recruitment of Ly6G+ cells, including neutrophils and monocytes, F4/80+ macrophages, and CD11c+ including macrophages and the dendritic cells in DSS-treated knockout mice, compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A reduced accumulation of primary bile acids alleviates experimental colitis in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Taken together, we propose that a reduced accumulation of primary bile acids alleviates experimental colitis in RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed correlation between reduced primary bile acids and reduced colitis severity.

claim: Daily supplementation of CDCA at the concentration of 10 mg/kg of body weight elevated the levels of CDCA in the colon without inducing any colitogenic phenotype in either wild-type or RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice even after 6 days.
source: Mere daily supplementation of CDCA at the concentration of 10 mg/kg of body weight, elevated the levels of CDCA in the colon (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b) without inducing any colitogenic phenotype in either wild-type or RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice even after 6 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by CDCA quantification and phenotypic assessment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b–e.

claim: The DAI of wild-type mice treated with both DSS and CDCA showed no change.
source: Moreover, the DAI of wild-type mice treated with both DSS and CDCA showed no change (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DAI measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CDCA supplementation of the DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed DAI equivalent to wild-type DSS-treated mice with concomitant supplementation of colon length shortening.
source: On the other hand, CDCA supplementation of the DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice showed DAI equivalent to wild-type DSS-treated mice with concomitant supplementation of colon length shortening (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DAI and colon length measurements shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Histological analyses of DSS-treated colon sections substantiated that CDCA supplementation together with DSS treatment was sufficient for imparting damage to the colonic crypts of the colitis-resistant RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Histological analyses of DSS-treated colon sections further substantiated that CDCA supplementation together with DSS treatment was sufficient for imparting damage to the colonic crypts of the colitis-resistant RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bile acid supplementation triggered a drastic reduction in the colonic abundance of mRNAs encoding the junctional proteins Tjp1 and Ocln as well as Muc2 in DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice.
source: Consistent with the observed intestinal pathologies, bile acid supplementation also triggered a drastic reduction in the colonic abundance of mRNAs encoding the junctional proteins Tjp1 and Ocln as well as Muc2 in DSS-treated RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Bile acid-supplemented RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice show prominently upregulated expression of genes encoding the pro-inflammatory cytokines Il1b, Tnfa, and Il6 upon DSS treatment, compared to those treated with DSS alone.
source: Concurrently, bile acid-supplemented RelaΔhepStat3Δhep mice show prominently upregulated expression of genes encoding the pro-inflammatory cytokines Il1b, Tnfa, and Il6 upon DSS treatment, compared to those treated with DSS alone (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: RelA and Stat3-driven accumulation of CDCA aggravates intestinal inflammation-induced damage during experimental colitis.
source: Thus, we conclude that RelA and Stat3-driven accumulation of CDCA aggravates intestinal inflammation-induced damage during experimental colitis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CDCA supplementation experiments showing restoration of colitis phenotype in knockout mice.

claim: IBD is a heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory intestinal disorders that are influenced by environmental cues, intestinal dysbiosis, and the local immune responses.
source: IBD is a heterogeneous group of chronic inflammatory intestinal disorders that are influenced by environmental cues, intestinal dysbiosis, and the local immune responses (Ananthakrishnan et al., 2018; de Souza and Fiocchi, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The conventional treatment regimen for IBD involves aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, and anti-TNF agents to counter bowel inflammation.
source: The conventional treatment regimen for IBD involves aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, and anti-TNF agents to counter bowel inflammation (Gómez-Gómez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) is known to induce inflammasome assembly by NF-κB/Lipocalin2-dependent axis in macrophages of colitogenic mice.
source: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS), one of the key components of microbial products, is known to induce inflammasome assembly by NF-κB/Lipocalin2-dependent axis in macrophages of colitogenic mice (Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LPS-mediated non-canonical Stat3 activation through TLR4 ligand reprograms metabolic and inflammatory pathways in macrophages.
source: Similarly, LPS-mediated non-canonical Stat3 activation through TLR4 ligand reprograms metabolic and inflammatory pathways in macrophages (Balic et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the acute DSS-induced colitis model, the release of LPS and other endotoxins would first activate kupffer cells of the liver, which then progressively triggers a response in relatively quiescent hepatocytes.
source: In the acute DSS-induced colitis model, the release of LPS and other endotoxins would first activate kupffer cells of the liver, which then progressively triggers a response in relatively quiescent hepatocytes (Taniki et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hepatic Rela and Stat3 have been reported to act cooperatively to render protection against pulmonary infection, by eliciting an acute phase response, which enhances the pulmonary immune response.
source: Previously, hepatic Rela and Stat3 have been reported to act cooperatively to render protection against pulmonary infection, by eliciting an acute phase response, which enhances the pulmonary immune response (Quinton et al., 2012; Hilliard et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hepatic functions of Rela and Stat3 amplify the immune response during experimental colitis, aggravating intestinal pathologies.
source: We observe similar hepatic functions of Rela and Stat3 that amplify the immune response during experimental colitis, aggravating intestinal pathologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations in this study.

claim: The primary bile acids are known to have inflammatory activity and the cardinal paradigm in IBD is the decreased levels of secondary bile acid.
source: The primary bile acids are known to have inflammatory activity and the cardinal paradigm in IBD is the decreased levels of secondary bile acid (Sinha et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Decreased levels of secondary bile acids in IBD has been attributed to the altered gut microflora that are known to convert primary BAs into secondary BAs.
source: This has been attributed to the altered gut microflora that are known to convert primary BAs into secondary BAs.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: A recent study that profiled the human intestinal environment under physiological conditions concluded that stool-based measurements do not reflect the true composition of BAs along the intestinal tracts.
source: It is important to note that most of these studies are carried out with fecal samples and a recent study that profiled the human intestinal environment under physiological conditions concluded that stool-based measurements do not reflect the true composition of BAs along the intestinal tracts.
evidence: The claim is supported by a reference to a recent study.

claim: Intestinal samples were dominated by primary BAs, whereas stool samples were dominated by secondary BAs.
source: Intestinal samples were dominated by primary BAs, whereas stool samples were dominated by secondary BAs (Shalon et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Analysis of colitogenic mice intestinal samples revealed enhanced primary BAs using mass spectrometry-based measurements.
source: Analysis of colitogenic mice intestinal samples also revealed enhanced primary BAs using mass spectrometry-based measurements.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from this study.

claim: Both CDCA and CA accumulate in the intestine and liver of colitogenic wild-type mice when compared to knockout littermates.
source: We observe both CDCA and CA accumulate in the intestine and liver of colitogenic wild-type mice when compared to knockout littermates.
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted LC-MS data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The accumulation of primary BA in both the intestine and liver is likely to be a consequence of increased biosynthesis in the liver and subsequent transport to the gut.
source: This accumulation of primary BA in both the intestine and liver is likely to be a consequence of increased biosynthesis in the liver and subsequent transport to the gut.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed accumulation of primary bile acids and upregulation of biosynthesis enzymes.

claim: Multiple primary bile synthesis pathway genes namely Cyp7a1, Cyp27a1, Cyp7b1, and Cyp8b1 were substantially upregulated in the liver of colitogenic wild-type mice.
source: Indeed, multiple primary bile synthesis pathway genes namely Cyp7a1, Cyp27a1, Cyp7b1, and Cyp8b1 were substantially upregulated in the liver.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The observation of upregulated bile synthesis genes is contradictory to the recently published work by Gui et al., 2023 which suggests that during IBD there is a downregulation of the biosynthesis machinery leading to reduced bile levels.
source: Our observation is contradictory to the recently published work by Gui et al., 2023 which suggests that during IBD there is a downregulation of the biosynthesis machinery leading to reduced bile levels.
evidence: The claim is a comparison with a previous study.

claim: Differences in observations may arise due to the dose of DSS, the time course of the experiment, and the mice strain adapted for different studies leading to the difference in the transcriptional and metabolic landscape during IBD.
source: Currently, we assume that these differences may arise due to the dose of DSS, the time course of the experiment, and the mice strain adapted for different studies leading to the difference in the transcriptional and metabolic landscape during IBD (Gui et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for differences with previous studies.

claim: Conventionally the cyp450 enzymes involved in the bile acid biosynthesis pathway are known to be regulated by the FXR signaling cascade.
source: Conventionally the cyp450 enzymes involved in the bile acid biosynthesis pathway are known to be regulated by the FXR signaling cascade (Eloranta and Kullak-Ublick, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: RelA and Stat3 transcriptionally control bile acid biosynthesis pathways under stress conditions.
source: Our data suggest that RelA and Stat3 transcriptionally control these pathways under stress conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed regulation of bile acid synthesis genes by Rela and Stat3.

claim: Increased CA has been attributed to colitis and CA was shown to limit the self-renewal capacity of intestinal stem cells leading to impaired intestinal restitution.
source: Previous studies of increased CA have been attributed to colitis and CA was shown to limit the self-renewal capacity of intestinal stem cells leading to impaired intestinal restitution (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Increased synthesis and secretion of the primary bile acids orchestrates intestinal inflammation.
source: We now propose that increased synthesis and secretion of the primary bile acids orchestrates intestinal inflammation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings in this study.

claim: This study identifies a hepatocyte-specific Rela-Stat3 network as a potential therapeutic target for intestinal diseases.
source: Thus our studies identify a hepatocyte-specific Rela/Stat3 network as a potential therapeutic target for intestinal diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: 30% of IBD cases have abnormal liver function tests and around 5% of them even develop chronic hepatobiliary diseases.
source: Clinically, IBD overlaps with hepatobiliary conditions, it has been reported that 30% of IBD cases have abnormal liver function tests and around 5% of them even develop chronic hepatobiliary diseases (Cappello et al., 2014; Gaspar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During colitis, the first responders to extraneous agents incoming from the leaky gut are the Kupffer cells.
source: During colitis, the first responders to extraneous agents incoming from the leaky gut are the Kupffer cells (Yamada et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Kupffer cells have been shown to switch from a pro to an anti-inflammatory state in response to signals received from the colitogenic gut.
source: These cells have been shown to switch from a pro to an anti-inflammatory state in response to signals received from the colitogenic gut (Taniki et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hepatocytes occupy ~80% of the liver.
source: Besides kuffer cells, the parenchymal cells, hepatocytes which occupy ~80% of the liver, also respond to these varied danger signals.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Hepatocytes are known to secrete a variety of factors like the complement proteins, clotting factors, hepatokines, bile acids, etc. which regulate local as well as distant organ functions.
source: Hepatocytes have a robust secretary machinery and are known to secrete a variety of factors like the complement proteins, clotting factors, hepatokines, bile acids, etc. which regulate local as well as distant organ functions (Kwon et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Albumin is the most abundantly produced serum protein by hepatocytes, which is implicated in the maintenance of redox balance and is known to attenuate DSS-induced colitis.
source: Among the secreted factors, albumin is the most abundantly produced serum protein, which is implicated in the maintenance of redox balance and is known to attenuate DSS-induced colitis (Yang et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: FNDC4 has the potential to reduce colonic inflammation by acting on the colonic macrophages.
source: Highlighting the importance of liver secretome, a recent study suggests that FNDC4 has the potential to reduce colonic inflammation by acting on the colonic macrophages (Bosma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Primary bile acids produced by the liver are often related to an enhanced proinflammatory state and its turnover to secondary bile acids is considered to be a critical step in the maintenance of homeostasis.
source: Similarly, bile acids are also known to play a pivotal role in regulating mucosal immune responses. Primary bile acids produced by the liver are often related to an enhanced proinflammatory state and its turnover to secondary bile acids is considered to be a critical step in the maintenance of homeostasis (Sun et al., 2021).
